prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Don't be misled: that sea-song you hear when the shell's at your ear? It's all in your head. That primordial tide— the slurp and salt-slosh of the brain's briny wash— is on the inside. Truth be told, the whole place, everything that the eye can take in, to the sky and beyond into space, lives inside of your skull. When you set your sad head down on Procrustes' bed, you lay down the whole universe. You recline on the pillow: the cosmos grows dim. The soft ghost in the squishy machine, which the world is, retires. Someday it will expire. Then all will go silent and dark. For the moment, however, the black- ness is just temporary. The planet you carry will shortly swing back from the far nether regions. And life will continue— but only within you. Which raises a question that comes up again and again, as to why God would make ear and eye to face outward, not in?

Here are three ways to polish the text, depending on your preferred format. All options preserve every original idea, image, and metaphor (including the ocean in the shell, the internal cosmos, Procrustes’ bed, the ghost in the machine, and the final philosophical question).

### Option 1: Elevated Literary Prose (Recommended)
*Best for an essay, speech, or philosophical article. It transforms the informal rhythm into elegant, sophisticated prose.*

> Do not be deceived: the ocean’s song heard when holding a shell to your ear resides entirely within your mind. That primordial tide—the ebb and flow of the brain’s briny fluids—originates from the inside. In truth, the entire expanse of existence—everything the eye can perceive, from the terrestrial horizon to the farthest reaches of space—lives strictly within the contours of your skull. 
>
> When you lay your weary head upon the bed of Procrustes, you lay down the universe itself. As you recline upon your pillow, the cosmos grows dim, and the spirit within this biological machine—the mind that constructs the world—temporarily retires. One day, it will cease entirely, casting all into absolute silence and darkness. For now, however, this obscurity is merely fleeting; the planet you carry will soon swing back from the nether regions of sleep, and life will resume—a life sustained exclusively within you. 
>
> This invites a persistent question: why would the Creator design the eyes and ears to face outward, rather than inward?

---

### Option 2: Refined Verse
*Best if you wish to keep the poetic, rhyming structure, but elevate the vocabulary and meter to sound more classical and articulate.*

> Do not be misled by the song in the shell,  
> For the ocean you hear is a secret to tell:  
> It is all in your head, a primordial tide,  
> The pulse of the brain’s briny waters inside.  
> 
> In truth, the vast realm that the eye can embrace—  
> Extending to skies and the reaches of space—  
> Is contained in the chamber that rests in your skull.  
> When you lie on Procrustes’ unforgiving bed,  
> The universe slumbers alongside your head.  
> 
> You rest on your pillow; the cosmos grows dim,  
> As the ghost in the mortal machine ceases hymn.  
> Though one day this spirit will finally expire,  
> And silence will smother the last fading fire,  
> For now, the deep darkness is merely a pause.  
> The planet you harbor defies night's own laws,  
> Returning to life, though contained in your mind—  
> 
> Which leaves a persistent enigma behind:  
> Why would the Maker mold ear and mold eye  
> To gaze on the world, not the soul deep inside?

---

### Option 3: Polished Hybrid (Rhythmic & Modern)
*Maintains the playful, rhythmic cadence of the original while replacing colloquial phrasing with more eloquent language.*

> Do not be misled: that sea-song you hear when a shell is at your ear? It is entirely in your mind. That primordial tide—the rhythmic wash of the brain’s internal sea—is purely an inside affair. 
>
> Truth be told, the entire expanse—everything the eye can capture, up to the heavens and far beyond into deep space—resides inside your skull. When you set your weary head down upon Procrustes' bed, you surrender the entire universe. You recline upon the pillow, and the cosmos grows dim. The subtle ghost within this complex machine—which constructs the world itself—retires for the night. 
>
> Someday, it will permanently expire, and all will go silent and dark. For the moment, however, the blackness is merely temporary. The planet you harbor will shortly swing back from those distant nether regions, and life will continue—yet only within you. Which raises a question that surfaces time and again: why would God design the ear and eye to face outward, rather than within?

---

### Key Improvements Made:
* **Refined Diction:** Words like *"slurp and salt-slosh"* were elevated to *"ebb and flow"* or *"rhythmic wash"*, and *"squishy machine"* was refined to *"biological machine"* or *"mortal machine"*.
* **Pacing & Flow:** Smoothed out sentence breaks to improve the natural cadence and reading experience.
* **Maintained Integrity:** Kept all specific references intact, including **Procrustes' bed**, the **ghost in the machine**, the **primordial/briny brain fluid**, and the final **theological query**.
outputs.L2:
Do not fall for the common illusion: the oceanic echo heard when pressing a shell against your ear originates entirely inside your own mind. What you are actually detecting is the internal sloshing of the salty fluid encased within your skull. 

In truth, the entire cosmos—ranging from everything your vision perceives around you to the open sky and distant cosmos—exists exclusively inside your head. Consequently, whenever you lay your weary head down to rest, you are essentially setting down the whole universe. As your head hits the pillow, your perception of reality fades, and the conscious mind animating your physical body temporarily steps away. 

Although a permanent silence and total pitch-blackness will eventually arrive when life ends, tonight’s darkness is merely brief. Shortly, the inner world you hold will return from the dark depths, allowing life to persist—yet solely within your own consciousness. This phenomenon naturally leads to a recurring puzzle: why would a divine creator design our visual and auditory organs to direct their attention outward rather than facing inward?
outputs.L3:
There is a poetic irony in the childhood pastime of holding a seashell to one’s ear to listen to the ocean. What feels like the distant, rhythmic surge of the tide is, in truth, a physiological illusion—the muted echo of blood coursing through our own vessels and the subtle hum of our own internal muscles. This misdirection serves as a fitting metaphor for the grander mechanics of human consciousness. 

The world we believe we inhabit is not, in fact, "out there" in the raw void. Every sight, sound, and sensation—from the immediate warmth of a room to the faint light of stars billions of light-years away—is a mental construct generated entirely within the dark, silent chamber of the human skull. The colors we perceive and the textures we touch are electrical signals translated by the brain. In a literal sense, the vast expanse of the cosmos does not surround us; rather, a private, intricate model of the universe unfolds entirely inside our own heads.

Nightly, this radiant internal universe undergoes a temporary eclipse. As we drift into sleep, the brain turns down the volume of sensory input, dimming the stars and dissolving the landscape of conscious thought. This routine passage into unconsciousness offers a quiet rehearsal for a final, permanent quietude. Sleep serves as a gentle foreshadowing of death—a brief taste of the absolute darkness that awaits when the internal projector finally turns off for good.

Yet, each morning, a quiet miracle takes place. Upon waking, the mind flickers back to life, instantly painting the universe back into existence. The walls of the bedroom materialize, daylight floods our consciousness, and the perceived cosmos is seamlessly restored. Reality resumes its function, allowing life to continue, lived out entirely within the self-contained architecture of the mind.

Recognizing the internal nature of reality brings us to a compelling philosophical paradox. If the universe we experience is generated entirely within the interior of the human mind, why are our sensory organs designed to face outward? Eyes, ears, and nerves reach constantly toward the exterior world, forever looking away from the very theater where our entire reality is being created.
outputs.L4:
Consider the ocean. You stand at the water's edge, listening to the rhythmic collapse of the surf, and you assume the sound belongs to the sea. Yet the crushing water itself moves in absolute, mechanical silence; the roar exists only when those mechanical waves collide with the delicate architecture of the inner ear, translating physical motion into a rushing tide of consciousness. Consider, too, the act of falling asleep. As the eyelids close, the physical room dissolves, yet vast landscapes, distant voices, and intricate dramas rise unbidden from the dark. In the dream state, we walk through worlds that require no physical ground to stand upon, proving that the mind possesses its own light, its own space, and its own geography.

These quiet, daily occurrences point toward a radical truth about the nature of perception: the universe as we experience it is an entirely internal phenomenon. The searing blue of a midsummer sky, the bitter cold of ice, the fragrance of crushed pine—none of these qualities exist in the external void. They are rendered, painted, and brought to life within the silent, dark interior of the human mind. Space itself, stretching out to the farthest, coldest galaxies, is a canvas stretched across the internal dome of human consciousness. We do not merely inhabit a world that exists outside of ourselves; rather, the world inhabits us. Reality is a grand theater whose only audience, and only stage, is the mind itself.

Yet, if all that we experience is generated within this internal sanctuary, a profound and troubling paradox presents itself—one rooted in our very anatomy. 

If the cosmos is fundamentally an internal creation, why is the human body built as though reality lay entirely elsewhere? Look at the physical architecture of the human face and form. Our eyes are set like forward-facing lanterns, gazing perpetually outward into the external gloom. Our ears are cupped like receivers, straining to catch vibrations from a distant void. Our nostrils flare toward the passing wind, and our skin reaches outward to grasp a world that lies beyond our borders. 

Here lies the magnificent irony of human existence: biology has turned us inside out. The instruments of our perception are physically oriented to look away from the very hearth where perception takes place. We are built like guardians standing at the tall windows of a magnificent hall, staring intently out into the dark courtyard, entirely oblivious to the fact that the entire universe is blazing brightly in the room behind us. We are vast, internal infinities, curiously equipped with senses that face the wrong way.
outputs.L5:
We spend much of our lives choosing what to wear—not merely the clothes on our backs, but the invisible armor we place around our hearts. Day after day, we don smiles when we are weary, don indifference when we are hurt, and don confidence when we are trembling inside. We wrap ourselves in carefully constructed narratives, hoping that if we play a role long enough, the persona will eventually become the person.

Yet, no matter how impeccably we craft the disguise, a quiet resonance remains beneath the surface. It is *that* subtle, persistent whisper that refuses to be drowned out by the noise of the world. It isn’t the loud distraction of daily routines, but *that* singular, undeniable moment of clarity waiting in the quiet hours of the night. It waits patiently for us to grow tired of the act.

When the weight of the armor finally becomes too heavy to carry, we are forced to strip away everything we don and look directly at what remains. In that bare, unvarnished space, we meet the truth. 

Truth is rarely convenient, and it seldom conforms to the comforting stories we tell ourselves. But beneath its sharp edges lies an undeniable liberation. When we stop hiding behind the disguises we choose to don, and finally look directly at *that* simple, unyielding truth, we find the one thing the pretense could never offer: peace.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming philosophical poem explaining that the sound of the ocean in a seashell is actually internal, expanding on the idea that the entire universe exists within our minds.
counterfactuals.output:
You lift the spiral to your ear,
And swear the distant tides draw near,
A calcified and hollow dome
That whispers of an ocean home.

Yet hold it still and listen deep:
It is no wave that breaks your sleep.
No cold Atlantic fills the turn,
No salty currents crash and churn;
It is the rhythm of your chest,
A quiet pulse that knows no rest.

The crimson rivers of your veins
Echo through those porcelain lanes.
The shell is but a subtle ring
That lets your own existence sing;
You hear no tempest on the coast,
Only your own internal ghost.

And if the sea you thought was real
Is just the heartbeat that you feel,
Then look beyond the shell to see
The nature of reality.
The starlit void, the burning sun,
And all the threads of space undone—

They do not bloom in light "out there,"
Suspended in a boundless air,
But glow within the neural maze,
A theater of thought and gaze.
The mind projects the earth and sky,
The canvas where the stars reply.

So listen close to what you hear,
The secret pressed against your ear:
You are the sea, the void, the ground,
The whisper and the hollow sound.
The universe, immense, divine,
Is folded in your mind's design.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a slightly dark, whimsical verse about solipsism and consciousness. Make sure to reference sleep, the "ghost in the machine," and end with a rhetorical question about human senses.
counterfactuals.output:
I stitched up the sky with a needle of thought,
And peopled the streets with the folk I begot.
They chatter and bleed, but they’re hollow within—
Just painted-on actors beneath paper skin.

A cog in the shadow, a spark in the dark,
The ghost in the machine leaves an oily black mark;
It pulls at the levers of muscle and bone
To dance in a ballroom it constructed alone.

And when I collapse into velvety sleep,
The universe melts to a silence so deep.
I wake, and it blooms like a poisonous rose:
A theatrical trick that my inner mind knows.

So if eyes only echo and ears only lie,
And touch is a spark that expires in a sigh,
If all I perceive is a myth I design,
How could I trust these five senses of mine?
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a short poem about perception versus reality using the ocean sound in a shell as the opening metaphor?
counterfactuals.output:
You press the spiral to your ear
And swear you hear the crashing sea,
A distant tide of endless blue
That whispers of infinity.

Yet no wild waves are trapped inside
This hollow, calcified retreat—
It’s but the rushing of your blood,
The rhythm of your own heart’s beat.

How easily the mind believes
The grand illusions we design:
We dream of oceans in a shell,
And mistake our echo for divine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of clever light verse exploring the question: if the universe is created inside our brains, why do our eyes and ears face outward?
counterfactuals.output:
The neuro-philosophers solemnly state
That the cosmos is built on an inside-out plate;
That the sun and the stars and the light on the sea
Are a trick of the mind, a synthetic "To Be."
The galaxy isn’t out there in the dark—
It’s a firing neuron, a chemical spark!
Three pounds of pink porridge, tucked under the crown,
Is constructing the universe, upside and down.

Which leads to a question both silly and sly,
A paradox suited to baffle the eye:
If the whole of creation is born in the mind,
Why aren't our senses directed *behind*?

Why mount our twin lenses to face at the street,
If the grand movie plays in the cerebrum's seat?
If ears gather tunes that the cortex composed,
Why point them *away* from the studio closed?

Imagine the nightmare if nature reversed,
And satisfied solipsists, better to worst!
If eyes swivelled inward to check on the plot,
They’d stare at a squishy and dark jelly-pot.
They’d scan through the meninges, peering at goo,
And whisper, "So *that’s* where I painted the view!"
And ears aimed inside would hear nothing but thumps,
And biochemical gurgles and vascular pumps.

No, the brain is a magician of marvelous talent,
Who likes to keep cosmic relations well-balanced.
It builds a projector, but hides the cassette,
And hangs out some windows so we don't forget.

It places two cameras out front on the hull,
To pretend that the world isn’t trapped in the skull.
For if we looked inward to see where it’s made,
We’d catch the projectionist spoiling the trade!

So our eyes look at daisies, our ears hear the bird,
To keep the illusion delightfully blurred.
The world is inside us—complete and entire—
But it puts on a puppet show out on the wire.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhyming poem about going to sleep that incorporates metaphors like Procrustes' bed, the brain's briny wash, and carrying a planet inside your skull.
counterfactuals.output:
The curtains draw, the hours lull,
I set my heavy burden down:
A spinning planet in my skull,
With every ocean, field, and town.
All day I bore this crowded sphere,
A world encased in bone and skin,
With all its gravity and fear
Locked in the atmosphere within.

Now night becomes Procrustes’ bed,
A standard frame where I must lie;
It trims the excess from my head
And cuts the day’s remaining tie.
It stretches out my restless frame,
Or chops the thoughts that grew too tall,
Adjusting every form and name
Until I fit the shadowy wall.

Then through the dark, the waters rise—
The brain’s deep, briny wash begins,
A saline tide behind my eyes
To scrub away the daily sins.
It sweeps through every grey ravine,
A cleansing sea in midnight's keep,
To rinse the worn engine clean
Before I sink into the deep.

The planet softens into air,
The rigid iron bed gives way;
Relieved of all the weight I bear,
I lose the remnants of the day.
The salt tide ebbs, the skull grows light,
The world inside dissolves to rest,
And I am folded in the night,
A quiet, unremembered guest.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
